MDdinner.mdDinner / drinks / lịch sự khi mời và từ chối · 67 lines⌄

Dinner and drinks

Dùng cho tối thứ Năm, sau workshop hoặc khi khách HQ sang Việt Nam. Lời mời nên thoải mái và luôn cho người khác cách từ chối.

Quick phrases

Situation Natural sentence Simpler alternative More professional alternative
Invite Are you joining us tonight? Coming tonight? We are having dinner after work. You are very welcome to join.
Time Shall we meet around seven? Seven o’clock? Would seven o’clock work for everyone?
Place It is a quiet place near the river. It is near the river. I picked somewhere quiet so we can talk comfortably.
Drink Would you like beer, wine, or something without alcohol? What would you like? What can I get you to drink?
Toast Cheers! It is good to have everyone here. Cheers! Cheers, and thank you for spending the evening with us.
Decline I will stay with sparkling water tonight. Water for me. I am not drinking tonight, but I am happy to join dinner.
Limit I will have just one tonight. Just one for me. I will keep it light tonight.
Leave I will head home after this one. I am leaving soon. I will call it a night after this drink.
Transport How are you getting home? Taxi home? Have you arranged transport back?
Close Thanks for tonight. I had a good time. Thanks. Good night. Thank you for a very enjoyable evening.

Realistic dialogue

Thursday drinks with colleagues

Colleague: Are we still going out tonight?
You: Yes, around seven. Would you like to join?
Colleague: Sure. Is it formal?
You: No, very casual. We will have food and one or two drinks.
Colleague: Great. I may leave early.
You: Of course. Come for as long as you like.
Colleague: Where are you going?
You: A quiet place near the river. I will send you the location.

With a visiting HQ manager

You: How has your week in Vietnam been so far?
Manager: Busy, but very interesting.
You: Have you had any time to explore the city?
Manager: Only a short walk near the hotel.
You: If you have time tomorrow, the river area is pleasant in the evening.
Manager: Good idea. Is it far from here?
You: About fifteen minutes by taxi, depending on traffic.

Leaving without making it awkward

Manager: Would you like another drink?
You: Thanks, but I will stop here. I have an early start tomorrow.
Manager: No problem.
You: I had a good time. How are you getting home?
Manager: I will book a car.
You: Great. Have a safe trip home. See you tomorrow.

Safe conversation topics

  • Food, travel, weekend plans, sports, books and city recommendations.
  • Ask about experience: “What did you enjoy most?”
  • Avoid pushing for personal details, alcohol or political opinions.

Useful vocabulary and collocations

  • a casual dinner — bữa tối thoải mái
  • go out for a drink — đi uống cùng nhau
  • keep it light — uống/ăn vừa phải
  • something without alcohol — đồ uống không cồn
  • make a toast — nâng ly chúc mừng
  • call it a night — kết thúc buổi tối
  • an early start — phải bắt đầu sớm hôm sau
  • get home safely — về nhà an toàn
MDlunch.mdLunch phrases / giới thiệu món ăn / nối chuyện công việc · 71 lines⌄

Lunch conversations

Mục tiêu: bắt đầu tự nhiên, chia sẻ một chi tiết của mình, hỏi tiếp một câu và kết thúc nhẹ nhàng. Dùng câu ngắn để vẫn rõ khi nhà hàng ồn.

Quick phrases

Situation Natural sentence Simpler alternative More professional alternative
Invite Shall we get lunch? Lunch? Would you like to join us for lunch?
Choose What do you feel like eating? What would you like? Do you have a preference today?
Recommend The grilled fish is good and not too spicy. The fish is good. I would recommend the grilled fish. It is quite mild.
Check diet Is there anything you do not eat? Any food you avoid? Do you have any dietary preferences?
Share I usually come here when I want something light. I come here sometimes. This is one of my usual places for a light lunch.
Ask back What do you normally have for lunch in France? What do you eat in France? What would a typical lunch be for you in France?
Work bridge After lunch, I would like your view on one point. Can I ask you something later? When we get back, could I get your view on one technical point?
Pay Shall we split the bill? Split the bill? Would you prefer to split the bill?
Time We should probably head back in ten minutes. Back in ten minutes? We have about ten minutes before the next meeting.
Close That was nice. Thanks for joining. Thanks. That was good. It was good catching up over lunch.

Realistic dialogue

Choosing a local dish

You: Shall we try the Vietnamese place today?
Manager: Yes. What do you recommend?
You: The grilled fish is good and not too spicy.
Manager: That sounds good. What comes with it?
You: Rice, vegetables and a light sauce. Do you eat much spicy food?
Manager: A little, but not too much.
You: Then this should be fine. I will order the same.

Talking about home cooking

Manager: Do you normally cook at home?
You: A few times a week. I usually make something simple.
Manager: What is your easiest dish?
You: Fried rice with vegetables. It is quick and hard to get wrong. What about you?
Manager: My wife usually cooks Japanese food.
You: Nice. Which dish do your children ask for when they come home?
Manager: Usually curry rice.
You: That is a good family meal.

Moving gently back to work

You: How is the food?
Manager: Very good. I like the sauce.
You: Me too. By the way, when we get back, could I get your view on the rollout plan?
Manager: Of course. What is the concern?
You: The rollback step is still unclear. I will show you the two options after lunch.
Manager: Good. Let us take ten minutes for it.
You: Perfect. No rush now. Let us finish lunch first.

When you do not hear clearly

  • Sorry, I missed the last part. What did you say about the dish?
  • Could you say the name again, a little more slowly?
  • Did you say rice or fries?
  • I know the place, but I have not tried that dish.

Useful vocabulary and collocations

  • grab lunch / get lunch — đi ăn trưa
  • something light — món nhẹ bụng
  • a filling dish — món ăn no
  • not too spicy — không quá cay
  • a local specialty — đặc sản địa phương
  • dietary preference — lựa chọn hoặc hạn chế ăn uống
  • split the bill — chia hóa đơn
  • head back — quay lại văn phòng
  • catch up over lunch — trò chuyện cập nhật trong bữa trưa
  • What comes with it? — món này ăn kèm gì?
MDsmall-talk.mdWarm-up trước meeting / small talk / chữa lỗi nghe · 69 lines⌄

Small talk

Small talk tốt nhất khi ngắn và liên quan đến tình huống hiện tại. Dùng công thức: mở câu → phản hồi chi tiết → chia sẻ một ý → chuyển chủ đề hoặc kết thúc.

Quick phrases

Moment Natural sentence Simpler alternative More professional alternative
Morning How is your morning going? Good morning so far? How has your morning been so far?
Busy day Is it a busy day for you? Busy today? Do you have a full schedule today?
Weekend Did you have a good weekend? Good weekend? Did you get a chance to relax over the weekend?
Weather The rain was heavy this morning. A lot of rain today. The weather made the journey in quite slow today.
Office Is this your first time in this office? First time here? Have you worked from this office before?
Event What did you think of the session? Good session? Was there anything from the session that stood out to you?
Fast speech Sorry, I missed the last part. Could you repeat that? Could you say that once more, a little more slowly?
Transition By the way, are you joining the next meeting? Next meeting? By the way, will you be joining the next session?
Close Good talking with you. See you later. See you later. It was good catching up. I will let you get back to your day.

Realistic dialogue

Before a meeting

You: Hi Claire, how is your week going?
Claire: Busy, but good. We have a release on Friday.
You: I know that feeling. We also have two reviews this week.
Claire: Good luck with those.
You: Thanks. Is Friday’s release a major one?
Claire: Mostly fixes, but one change is quite sensitive.
You: I hope it goes smoothly. Shall we get ready for the meeting?

Meeting a Singapore colleague

You: Hi Daniel, good to meet you in person. How was the flight?
Daniel: Short and easy, thanks.
You: Is this your first visit to our office?
Daniel: Yes. The area has changed a lot since my last trip to Vietnam.
You: It changes quickly. If you need lunch or transport suggestions, let me know.
Daniel: Thanks, I appreciate that.

Corridor conversation with a senior manager

Manager: How are things going?
You: Good overall. I am reviewing two projects this week.
Manager: Any major concerns?
You: One deployment risk needs attention, but the team has a clear action plan.
Manager: Good to hear.
You: I will keep you posted if the risk changes. Enjoy the rest of your day.

Joining a group conversation

Colleague: We were just talking about weekend plans.
You: Nice. Is anyone going somewhere interesting?
Colleague: Marie is going to Da Lat.
You: Great choice. It should be cooler there. Have you been before, Marie?
Marie: No, it is my first time.
You: Then the coffee farms may be worth a visit.

Conversation repair

  • Sorry, I did not catch the name of the place.
  • I heard the first part, but I missed the end.
  • When you say “next week”, do you mean Monday or later in the week?
  • Let me check that I understood you correctly.

Useful collocations

  • a full schedule, a quiet weekend, heavy traffic, catch up
  • stand out, go smoothly, keep someone posted, join a conversation
  • get back to your day, good to meet you in person, first time here
MDtravel.mdBusiness trip / holiday / điểm đến · 63 lines⌄

Travel conversations

Travel là chủ đề dễ dùng với đồng nghiệp Pháp và Singapore. Hỏi một câu, phản hồi vào chi tiết vừa nghe rồi chia sẻ ngắn về mình.

Quick phrases

Situation Natural sentence Simpler alternative More professional alternative
Recent trip How was your trip? Good trip? How did the trip go overall?
Business trip Was the schedule very busy? Busy schedule? Did you have much time between meetings?
Summer Are you planning any trips this summer? Any summer travel? Do you have plans for the summer break?
Family Are you travelling with the family? Family trip? Will the whole family be travelling together?
Duration How long are you staying? How many days? How long will you be there this time?
Recommend If you like quiet places, try Ninh Binh. Try Ninh Binh. If you prefer somewhere quieter, Ninh Binh is worth considering.
Transport It is easier to get around by metro. Take the metro. The metro is probably the easiest way to get around.
Weather It can be very humid in the afternoon. Afternoons are humid. I would plan outdoor activities for the morning.
Return When do you get back? Back when? When will you be back in the office?
Wish Have a great trip. Enjoy your trip. I hope you and your family have a wonderful trip.

Realistic dialogue

Manager’s summer holiday

You: Do you have any travel plans this summer?
Manager: We may spend three weeks in Japan.
You: That sounds lovely. Will you visit family as well?
Manager: Yes, for a few days, then we will travel around.
You: Which area are you most looking forward to?
Manager: Probably Hokkaido. It should be cooler there.
You: Good choice. The summer here will be very hot.

Colleague returning from France

You: Welcome back. How was the trip?
Colleague: Good, but the flight was long.
You: Did you manage to sleep on the plane?
Colleague: Only for two hours.
You: That is tough. I hope your afternoon is not too busy.
Colleague: Luckily, I only have one meeting.

Helping a visitor plan a weekend

Visitor: I have Saturday free. Where should I go?
You: Do you prefer the city, the beach or somewhere quiet?
Visitor: Somewhere quiet, with good scenery.
You: I would suggest Ninh Binh. It is better for an overnight trip.
Visitor: Is it easy to get there?
You: Yes. A private car is the simplest option if your time is limited.

Follow-up questions

  • What was the best part of the trip?
  • Was anything different from what you expected?
  • Would you go back?
  • Which place would you recommend for a first visit?
  • Did you find any good local food?

Useful collocations

  • summer break, business trip, direct flight, connecting flight
  • travel light, pack for the weather, get around, avoid rush hour
  • worth a visit, less crowded, an overnight trip, a first-time visitor
  • look forward to, get back, recover from jet lag
MDEnglish_TA.mdTechnical Advisor đầy đủ: vai trò, AI adoption, kỹ thuật và leadership · 1,604 lines⌄

English for a Technical Advisor

Purpose

This guide is for a Technical Advisor who works with developers, product teams, project managers, business stakeholders, customers, and other technical teams.

The goal is to help you speak in a way that is:

  • clear and professional;
  • technical without sounding too complex;
  • collaborative rather than controlling;
  • suitable for international teams;
  • easy to adapt for French and wider European work culture;
  • useful in daily work, meetings, reviews, troubleshooting, and decision-making.

A Technical Advisor is not only someone who knows technology. The role is often to understand the situation, ask the right questions, compare options, identify risks, guide the team, and help people make a good technical decision.

1. How to describe your role

Short version

I work as a Technical Advisor. I help the team analyze technical topics, review solution options, identify risks, and make practical decisions.

Natural version

My role is to support the team on technical decisions. I usually help clarify the problem, review possible solutions, check constraints and risks, and make sure the proposed approach fits the wider system.

More senior version

I act as a technical point of reference for the team. I help connect business needs with technical reality, challenge assumptions when needed, and support teams in choosing solutions that are realistic, maintainable, and aligned with our standards.

When speaking with non-technical people

I help translate technical topics into clear options, risks, and next steps so that the team can make informed decisions.

When speaking with developers

I am here to support the technical direction, review options, help unblock difficult topics, and make sure we consider the impact beyond the immediate implementation.

2. How to answer the AI coding survey as a Technical Advisor

Question 1

How are you using AI coding tools in your day-to-day work right now?

Option A

I use AI coding tools to analyze technical issues, review implementation approaches, troubleshoot problems, and understand unfamiliar code more quickly. I also use them to prepare technical notes, compare solution options, and support discussions with developers.

Option B

I mainly use AI as a technical assistant. It helps me explore possible solutions, validate my understanding, review code or logs, and prepare clearer explanations for the team.

Option C

I use AI coding tools to speed up technical analysis, investigate incidents, review design ideas, and prepare examples or documentation. I do not rely on the output directly; I always check it against the project context and technical constraints.

Question 2

How confident are you that AI coding tools are making you more productive?

Recommended choice:

Confident

Use Very confident only if AI already saves you a significant amount of time in your daily work.

Question 3

How would you describe your working relationship with AI coding tools?

Option A

I use AI coding tools as a technical thought partner. They help me explore options and challenge assumptions, while I use my own experience and project context to validate the result.

Option B

I see AI as an assistant rather than a final decision-maker. It helps me work faster, but I still review the technical details, risks, and impact before recommending a solution.

Option C

I use AI to support my analysis and prepare ideas, but the final recommendation still depends on architecture, security, business needs, and the team’s experience.

Question 4

What’s getting in the way of you or your team using AI coding tools more effectively?

Option A

The main challenge is giving AI enough business, technical, and architectural context. Without that context, the answer can be technically correct but not suitable for our environment.

Option B

Accuracy, data privacy, and project context are the main concerns. We also need clear ways to validate AI-generated suggestions before using them in real systems.

Option C

AI can be useful, but it does not always understand our internal constraints, legacy systems, or team standards. Better integration with project context would make it more effective.

Question 5

When AI-generated code isn’t right, what do you usually do first?

Recommended answer:

Debug it together with the AI

Alternative:

Reprompt with more detail

Both fit a Technical Advisor role because they show that you first clarify the issue instead of accepting the result without review.

Question 6

What are you hoping to get out of this program?

Option A

I would like to improve how I use AI for technical analysis, troubleshooting, solution evaluation, and developer collaboration. I also want to learn how to get more reliable results while using AI responsibly.

Option B

I want to learn better ways to use AI as part of technical decision-making, especially for investigation, architecture discussions, code review, and problem solving.

Option C

I am interested in practical methods for using AI in real technical work, while keeping good engineering judgment, security, and maintainability in mind.

3. Daily phrases for a Technical Advisor

Starting a technical discussion

Let me make sure I understand the issue correctly.

Can we first agree on the problem we are trying to solve?

Before we go into the solution, I would like to understand the current behavior.

Could you walk me through the flow from start to finish?

What is the main constraint here?

Is this a technical limitation, a business rule, or both?

What changed before the issue started?

Do we know whether this is isolated or affecting several components?

Let us separate the symptom from the root cause.

I think we should first clarify the expected behavior.

Asking for more context

Could you give me a bit more context?

Do we have an example from production?

Can you share the logs or error message?

Which service owns this part of the flow?

Is this behavior documented somewhere?

Has this happened before?

What assumptions are we making here?

Do we know the expected volume?

Are there any security or compliance constraints?

Is there a deadline that affects the solution?

4. Giving technical advice without sounding too strong

A Technical Advisor often needs to influence without sounding like they are giving orders.

Direct but collaborative

Instead of:

We have to do it this way.

Say:

I would recommend this approach because it gives us a clearer separation of responsibilities.

Instead of:

This solution is wrong.

Say:

I see a few risks with this approach. Maybe we can review them before we decide.

Instead of:

Do not use this.

Say:

I would be careful with this option because it could create issues later.

Instead of:

This will not work.

Say:

I am not sure this will work well under the current constraints.

Instead of:

You need to change the design.

Say:

I think the design could benefit from one small adjustment.

5. Common meeting language

Opening a meeting

Thanks everyone for joining.

The goal today is to agree on the technical direction.

I suggest we focus on the main decision first and keep smaller details for later.

I would like to make sure we leave the meeting with clear next steps.

We have a few options to review today.

Maybe we can start with the current situation and then discuss the proposed change.

Structuring the discussion

I see three points we need to cover.

First, let us look at the current behavior.

Second, we should review the main risks.

Finally, we can agree on the preferred option.

I suggest we separate short-term fixes from the long-term solution.

Maybe we can look at this from both the application side and the infrastructure side.

There are two different questions here.

Let us take them one by one.

Bringing the team back on topic

I think this is useful, but maybe slightly outside today’s scope.

Can we park this point and come back to the main question?

I suggest we keep this as a follow-up item.

Maybe we are going too deep into implementation details for now.

For today, I think we only need to agree on the direction.

6. Showing your Technical Advisor role in meetings

These phrases help other people clearly see that you are guiding the technical discussion.

Clarifying the problem

Before recommending a solution, I would like to confirm the real source of the issue.

From what I understand, the technical problem is not the API itself but the way the data is handled after the response.

I think we have two different concerns here: reliability and performance.

The current issue seems to be a combination of configuration and application behavior.

Comparing options

We have two realistic options.

Option A is simpler and faster, but it gives us less flexibility later.

Option B needs more work now, but it is easier to maintain in the long term.

Technically, both options are possible. The main difference is cost, complexity, and operational impact.

I would prefer the second option if we expect this area to grow.

For a short-term fix, the first option is acceptable.

Highlighting risks

The main risk I see is around backward compatibility.

We should also consider the operational impact.

My concern is not the implementation itself, but how this behaves under higher load.

This is technically possible, but it increases dependency between the two services.

We should be careful not to introduce a temporary fix that becomes permanent.

I would like us to check the security impact before we proceed.

This could work, but we need a rollback plan.

Making a recommendation

Based on the current constraints, I would recommend option B.

My preference would be to keep the change as small as possible.

I think the safest approach is to validate this with a small proof of concept first.

From a maintenance point of view, I would choose the simpler design.

If there is no strong business reason to customize this, I would stay close to the standard solution.

7. How to disagree professionally

This is especially useful in French and European teams, where directness is often accepted, but it is better to stay factual and respectful.

Soft disagreement

I see your point, but I have a slightly different view.

I understand the idea. My concern is mainly about the long-term impact.

That could work. I am just not fully convinced about the operational side.

I agree with the objective, but I am not sure about the proposed implementation.

I think we may be solving the right problem in a more complex way than necessary.

Stronger disagreement

I would not recommend this approach in the current setup.

I think this creates more risk than value.

From a technical point of view, I do not think we have enough evidence to proceed with this option.

I would prefer that we validate the assumption before making this change.

I think we should challenge this design before we commit to it.

When you need to say no

I do not think we should move forward with this yet.

I would be uncomfortable approving this without additional testing.

At this stage, I cannot recommend this solution.

We can do it, but I think we need to be clear about the trade-offs first.

I would prefer to keep this out of production until we have validated the failure scenario.

8. French / European communication style

There is no single European style, but in many French and European workplaces, people often appreciate communication that is:

  • clear;
  • factual;
  • not overly enthusiastic;
  • respectful of expertise;
  • open to debate;
  • careful with commitments;
  • focused on reasoning and trade-offs.

You can sound professional without using too many positive words.

Instead of very American-style enthusiasm

Instead of:

Amazing idea! I love it!

Use:

Yes, that could be a good option.

Or:

That makes sense to me.

Or:

I think this is worth exploring.

Instead of:

Absolutely, this is perfect.

Use:

Yes, I agree with the direction.

Or:

This looks reasonable.

Or:

I think this is a solid approach.

Instead of:

Great job, everyone!

Use:

Thanks everyone. I think we made good progress.

Or:

Thanks, this gives us a clear direction.

Neutral and professional

I have no major concern with this option.

I would like to challenge one assumption.

Maybe we should verify this before moving forward.

I suggest we keep the solution simple.

I think we should avoid adding complexity unless we really need it.

Can we agree on this as the next step?

I am comfortable with this direction.

Polite but not too formal

Would it make sense to check this first?

Maybe we can look at another option as well.

I would be interested to hear the team’s view.

Do you see any issue with this approach?

Does anyone see a constraint I may have missed?

I am happy to review this with you.

We can discuss it offline if useful.

10. Technical review conversations

Reviewing a design

Developer: We are thinking about calling the service directly from the frontend.

Technical Advisor:

Technically that is possible, but I would like to check the security and dependency impact first. What is the reason for bypassing the backend in this case?

Developer: It would be faster to implement.

Technical Advisor:

I understand. For a short-term solution, that may be attractive. My concern is that it could make authentication and future changes harder. Could we compare both options before deciding?

Reviewing an API change

Developer: We need to add three new fields to the API.

Technical Advisor:

That sounds reasonable. Are the fields optional or required?

Developer: Required.

Technical Advisor:

In that case, we should check backward compatibility. Do we know whether existing consumers can handle the change?

Developer: Not yet.

Technical Advisor:

Then I would suggest validating the consumers first. If needed, we could introduce the fields as optional and make them mandatory later.

11. Troubleshooting conversations

Production incident

Team member: The service is returning 500 errors.

Technical Advisor:

Do we know when it started?

Team member: Around 10:30.

Technical Advisor:

Was there any deployment or configuration change around that time?

Team member: There was a deployment at 10:15.

Technical Advisor:

Okay. I would first compare the logs before and after the deployment. We should also check whether the error affects all requests or only a specific flow.

When the root cause is unclear

At the moment, I do not think we have enough information to call this a database issue.

Let us verify the application logs first.

Can we reproduce the issue outside production?

I would like to rule out configuration before we change the code.

Let us collect the evidence first and then decide where to focus.

12. Architecture discussions

Introducing an architecture point

I would like to look at this from a system perspective.

This works locally, but we should also consider how it fits into the wider architecture.

My main question is where this responsibility should live.

We should avoid creating unnecessary coupling between these components.

I think ownership is important here.

Which team will maintain this component in the long term?

Discussing scalability

The current design should work for today’s volume.

The question is whether we expect the traffic to grow significantly.

Do we have an estimate for peak load?

We do not need to over-engineer this, but we should avoid a clear bottleneck.

I would keep the design simple and monitor before adding more complexity.

13. Security and compliance discussions

Before we proceed, I would like to confirm the data classification.

Does this flow contain personal or sensitive data?

Are we allowed to send this information to an external service?

We should confirm the retention requirements.

I would like security to review this point.

This looks technically fine, but we should still check the compliance impact.

We should avoid logging sensitive information.

Can we mask this value in the logs?

14. Talking to project managers

Explaining technical risk

The implementation itself is not very complex, but there is some uncertainty around integration.

The main risk is not development time; it is testing across the dependent systems.

We can meet the date, but we may need to reduce the scope.

I would prefer not to commit to the final date until we confirm the dependency.

From a technical side, the timeline is possible if the interface remains stable.

Asking for prioritization

We have two technical issues, but only one is blocking the release.

Could we confirm which one has higher business priority?

If the deadline is fixed, we may need to choose the simpler option.

We can do both, but not with the same level of depth in the current timeline.

15. Talking to business stakeholders

Explaining a technical limitation

The request is possible, but it requires a change in the way the current system is designed.

We can support this scenario, but it will take more effort than a normal configuration change.

The current platform does not support this directly.

We have a workaround, but I would not recommend it as a long-term solution.

We need to understand how important this requirement is before choosing the technical approach.

Explaining trade-offs

We can make it faster, or we can make it more flexible, but doing both will increase complexity.

The simpler solution is easier to maintain but has fewer customization options.

The more advanced option gives us more flexibility, but it will require more testing and support.

There is no technical blocker. It is mainly a question of cost, time, and long-term maintenance.

16. Talking to a customer

When you need more information

To understand the issue better, could you share one example where the behavior is incorrect?

Could you confirm the expected result?

Do you know when the problem first appeared?

Is the issue happening for all users or only some users?

If possible, could you provide the timestamp and request ID?

When you do not know yet

I do not want to give you an incorrect answer, so I would like to verify this point first.

We are still investigating the root cause.

We have identified one possible cause, but we need to confirm it.

I will review this with the team and come back with a clear recommendation.

At this stage, I would prefer not to speculate.

17. Working with senior engineers

I would like your view on one point.

Do you see any architectural concern with this option?

I have reviewed the main flow, but I would appreciate a second opinion on the failure scenario.

My current recommendation is option A, mainly because it reduces coupling.

I may be missing some historical context here.

18. Working with junior developers

A Technical Advisor should guide without taking over all the work.

What have you tried so far?

What do you think is the root cause?

Which part of the flow are you least confident about?

Let us go through the logic together.

Your approach is reasonable. I would just add one check here.

Before changing the code, how could we confirm the assumption?

Can you think of a failure case for this design?

Try to keep the first version simple.

Once you have a first proposal, I am happy to review it with you.

19. Code review phrases

Positive

This looks clear to me.

The logic is easy to follow.

I like that the change is small and focused.

This is simpler than the previous version.

The error handling looks better now.

Suggestions

Could we simplify this part?

Do we need this additional abstraction?

Would it be clearer to move this logic into a separate function?

Could we add a test for the failure case?

What happens if this value is null?

Is there a reason we are catching the exception here?

Could this affect existing consumers?

I would add a short comment explaining why this behavior is needed.

Concerns

I am slightly concerned about the dependency introduced here.

This may become difficult to maintain.

I think we should avoid duplicating this logic.

This could create inconsistent behavior between the two flows.

I would prefer not to merge this until we confirm the edge case.

20. When someone asks for your opinion

Instead of always saying “I think”, vary your language.

My view is that we should keep the current design.

From a technical perspective, option B is safer.

Based on what we know today, I would choose option A.

My preference would be to avoid another dependency.

The way I see it, the main issue is ownership.

For me, the key point is maintainability.

I would lean toward the simpler approach.

I am comfortable with either option, but option B gives us more flexibility.

21. When you are not fully sure

I need to verify that.

I am not completely sure about that behavior.

My understanding is that it works this way, but I would like to confirm.

I believe this is configurable, but let me check.

I do not have enough information to answer confidently yet.

I would rather confirm before giving a final recommendation.

This style is often better than pretending to know.

22. When someone interrupts you

Let me just finish this point.

I will come to that in a second.

Yes, that is related. Let me complete the current point first.

I think we are saying something similar. Let me clarify what I mean.

Maybe I did not explain that clearly.

23. When you interrupt politely

Sorry to interrupt, but can I clarify one point?

Just one quick question before we continue.

Can I stop you there for a second?

Before we move on, could we confirm one thing?

I think this point may affect the rest of the discussion.

24. When the discussion becomes too complex

I think we are mixing several topics.

Maybe we can simplify the question.

Let us focus on what we actually need for the first version.

We may be over-engineering this.

I suggest we start with the minimum solution and add complexity only if needed.

Can we draw the flow? It may be easier to see the issue.

25. Decision-making phrases

Before the decision

Do we have enough information to decide today?

Is there any major concern we have not discussed?

Are we comfortable with the risk?

Do we need input from another team?

Is there any blocker to choosing this option?

Confirming the decision

It sounds like we are aligned on option B.

So the decision is to keep the existing API and update the backend logic.

Just to confirm, we will proceed with the simpler option for the first release.

I think we have a clear direction.

Unless there is an objection, I suggest we proceed with this approach.

26. Ending a meeting

Let me summarize the next steps.

We agreed on the technical direction.

The remaining open point is the security review.

I will document the decision and the main reasons behind it.

Could you take the action on the API change?

I will follow up with the infrastructure team.

Let us review the result once the proof of concept is ready.

Thanks everyone. I think we have what we need for now.

27. Follow-up messages after meetings

Simple follow-up

Thanks for the discussion today.
We agreed to proceed with option B.
The main reasons are lower dependency and easier maintenance.
The remaining action is to confirm the security impact before implementation.

More formal European style

Thank you for the discussion.
As agreed, we will proceed with the proposed backend change while keeping the existing API contract.
Before implementation, we still need confirmation from Security regarding data handling.
Please let me know if I missed anything.

Short Teams/Slack message

Thanks all. We are aligned on option B. I will update the technical note and add the open security point.

28. Asking another team for help

We are reviewing an issue that may involve your service.

Could someone from your team help us confirm the expected behavior?

We would like to understand whether this is a known limitation.

Could you help us validate the configuration on your side?

We are not asking for a change yet; we first want to confirm the current behavior.

If useful, I can share a short summary of what we have found so far.

29. Handling ownership questions

Which team currently owns this component?

Who should be the long-term owner of this logic?

I think we should clarify ownership before adding more functionality here.

Technically we can implement it in either place, but ownership should influence the decision.

I would prefer the logic to stay with the team that owns the business rule.

30. Handling deadlines

What is the real deadline for this change?

Is the date fixed, or is there some flexibility?

If the date cannot move, we should reduce the technical scope.

I can support the short-term solution, but we should document the follow-up work.

I do not want the temporary solution to become the default architecture.

We can deliver a safe first version and improve it after the release.

31. Handling pressure

When someone asks you to approve something quickly:

I understand the urgency, but I would like to check one risk before approving it.

I can give a provisional view now, but I would prefer to confirm after reviewing the logs.

I do not want to block the team unnecessarily, but this point needs validation.

If we proceed now, we should be clear about the risk we are accepting.

32. When a meeting has too many opinions

I think we have several valid views.

Maybe we should compare the options using the same criteria.

Could we agree on the decision criteria first?

For me, the main criteria are maintainability, delivery time, and operational risk.

If we use those criteria, option B seems stronger.

This helps you act as an advisor rather than another person adding an opinion.

33. Useful decision criteria

When comparing technical solutions, you can mention:

  • implementation effort;
  • maintainability;
  • reliability;
  • security;
  • performance;
  • scalability;
  • operational complexity;
  • cost;
  • dependency;
  • ownership;
  • supportability;
  • backward compatibility;
  • user impact;
  • delivery time.

Example:

If we compare the two options in terms of effort, maintainability, and operational risk, I think option A is the better fit.

Can you see my screen?

Could you repeat the last point?

I may have missed part of that.

35. Daily stand-up examples

Example 1

Yesterday I reviewed the integration issue and identified two possible causes. Today I will validate the API behavior with the platform team. At the moment, there is no blocker, but we still need confirmation on one configuration point.

Example 2

I supported the team on the authentication issue and reviewed the proposed fix. The code change looks small, but I asked for one additional test before we close the topic.

Example 3

I am currently reviewing the solution for the new data flow. The main open question is ownership between the two services. I will discuss that with both teams today.

36. Sprint planning examples

From a technical side, this story looks feasible.

I think we should add one task for integration testing.

There is one dependency that may affect the estimate.

Before we commit, can we confirm whether the API is already available?

I would keep some time for investigation because the legacy behavior is not fully documented.

The implementation is straightforward, but the testing scope is wider than the code change.

37. Refinement meeting examples

The requirement is clear at a high level, but I think we need one more detail about error handling.

What should happen if the external service is unavailable?

Do we need to support partial success?

Is this behavior expected for existing users as well?

Could we add an acceptance criterion for this case?

38. Retrospective examples

From my side, the main issue was that we discovered the dependency too late.

I think earlier technical alignment would have reduced the rework.

One thing that worked well was involving the platform team early.

Next time, I suggest we validate external dependencies during refinement.

I do not think we need a large process change; one additional technical check should be enough.

39. Incident review / post-mortem examples

The immediate cause was the configuration change, but the deeper issue was that we did not have validation for this scenario.

I would avoid focusing only on the individual change.

We should ask why the system allowed this failure to reach production.

I suggest we add monitoring for this condition.

The goal is not to add more process, but to detect the problem earlier.

I think one automated check would prevent the same issue from happening again.

40. Change approval examples

I have reviewed the change and I am comfortable with the technical approach.

I have one condition before approval: we need a rollback plan.

The change is low risk as long as the configuration is deployed first.

I would recommend testing this in staging with production-like data.

I am okay to proceed once the monitoring is in place.

41. Vendor or external partner meetings

Could you explain how this feature behaves in a failure scenario?

Is this limitation documented?

What is the recommended architecture for this integration?

Do you support this configuration in production?

Is there any known performance limit?

How do other customers usually handle this use case?

Could you share the official recommendation after the meeting?

42. When you want to challenge a vendor

I understand that this is the standard recommendation, but I am not sure it fits our architecture.

Could you explain the reason behind this limitation?

Is there a technical reason this cannot be supported?

Do you have any reference architecture for a similar environment?

I would like to understand the trade-off before we adopt this approach.

43. Email language

Asking for review

Subject: Technical review – proposed integration approach

Hi all,
I have added a short proposal for the integration approach.
The main points to review are service ownership, error handling, and backward compatibility.
Please add any comments before Thursday if possible.
Thanks.

Raising a concern

Subject: Technical concern – dependency between Service A and Service B

Hi all,
During the review, I noticed that the proposed design introduces a direct dependency between Service A and Service B.
This is technically possible, but it may make future changes and incident handling more difficult.
I suggest we review one alternative before finalizing the design.
Thanks.

Confirming a decision

Subject: Decision – API change approach

Hi all,
Following today’s discussion, we agreed to keep the existing API contract and make the change in the backend.
This gives us lower consumer impact and a simpler rollout.
The only remaining action is to confirm the security review.
Please let me know if I missed anything.

These work well when you want to sound calm, professional, and not too sales-oriented.

47. Mini dialogues for common situations

A. Developer asks for quick approval

Developer: Can we merge this today?

Technical Advisor:

The change looks reasonable. I just want to confirm the error handling before we merge. If that is covered, I am fine to proceed.

B. PM asks if the feature can be delivered

PM: Can we deliver this by Friday?

Technical Advisor:

The core change is possible by Friday. The risk is the integration testing. If the date is fixed, I suggest we keep the first version limited to the main flow.

C. Business asks for customization

Business: Can we make the behavior different for this customer?

Technical Advisor:

Yes, technically we can. Before we do that, I would like to understand whether this is a one-off need or something we expect for other customers as well. That will affect the design.

D. Team proposes a complex architecture

Developer: We can add a new service for this.

Technical Advisor:

We can, but I am not sure we need another service for this scope. Could we first see whether the existing component can own the logic without creating a strong dependency?

E. Incident with little information

Manager: Do we know the cause?

Technical Advisor:

Not yet. We have one possible lead, but I would not call it the root cause yet. We are checking the logs and the latest deployment first.

48. Phrases that make your role visible

Use these naturally, not all the time.

I would like to look at the wider technical impact.

Let us make sure the solution fits the existing architecture.

I want to separate what is technically possible from what is advisable.

We should consider not only implementation but also support and maintenance.

The question for me is whether this is the right responsibility for this component.

I would like to understand the trade-offs before recommending an option.

My role here is mainly to help the team choose the safest practical approach.

I am happy to challenge the design if that helps us avoid problems later.

49. Things to avoid

Try not to overuse:

Obviously...

Clearly...

You are wrong.

This makes no sense.

We always do it this way.

That is not my problem.

Just do it.

Trust me.

This is easy.

These phrases can sound dismissive, especially in international teams.

Prefer:

My understanding is...

I see it differently.

Could we review the reason for this choice?

I think there is another option.

Let us check the impact first.

50. Simple formula for speaking like a Technical Advisor

A useful structure is:

Context → Observation → Risk → Recommendation → Next step

Example:

We currently call the external API directly from two services.
I noticed that both services implement the same retry logic.
This may lead to inconsistent behavior and make support more difficult.
I would recommend moving the retry policy to a shared integration layer.
As a next step, we can prepare a small design proposal and review the impact.

This structure makes your communication clear and senior without using difficult vocabulary.

51. Another useful formula for meetings

Question → Evidence → Options → Decision

Example:

The question is where the validation logic should live.
Today, the same rule is already used by three services.
We can either keep the logic in each service or centralize it.
I would recommend centralizing it because the rule is shared and likely to change.

52. Quick phrase bank

Clarify

Could you clarify that point?

What exactly do we mean by this?

What is the expected behavior?

Analyze

Let us look at the root cause.

I see two possible explanations.

We should verify the assumption.

Recommend

I would recommend the simpler option.

My preference is to keep the current interface.

I suggest we validate this first.

Challenge

I would like to challenge one assumption.

Do we really need this complexity?

What problem does this additional layer solve?

Align

Are we aligned on the approach?

Can we agree on this direction?

Does anyone have a major concern?

Close

I think we have a clear next step.

I will document the decision.

Let us review again after the test.

53. A natural personal introduction

Hi, I am working as a Technical Advisor. I support teams on technical analysis, solution design, troubleshooting, and technical decision-making. I often work across different teams to clarify issues, review options, and make sure solutions are practical and maintainable.

A more relaxed version:

I am a Technical Advisor. I mainly help teams with technical decisions, complex issues, and solution reviews. I also work with developers and stakeholders to make sure we understand the problem correctly before choosing an approach.

54. Final communication principles

As a Technical Advisor:

  1. Ask before assuming.
  2. Separate facts from opinions.
  3. Explain risks without creating unnecessary fear.
  4. Give options when possible.
  5. Recommend, do not command.
  6. Say when you need to verify something.
  7. Keep technical language simple when speaking with non-technical people.
  8. Explain trade-offs, not only solutions.
  9. Make decisions and next steps clear.
  10. Stay calm and factual when the discussion becomes difficult.

A useful sentence to remember:

My goal is not only to find a solution that works today, but to help the team choose one that we can understand, support, and maintain tomorrow.

MDFood_Travel_SmallTalk_Vietnam_France_Playbook(1).mdFood, travel và VN–FR social: món ăn cụ thể, coffee, hội thoại · 529 lines⌄

Food, Travel & Small-Talk Playbook

Practical English for Vietnamese–French workplace conversations

Mục tiêu: dùng khi ăn trưa, dinner, uống bia, đi công tác, đón đồng nghiệp/sếp nước ngoài, hoặc small talk trước/sau meeting. Ưu tiên câu ngắn, dễ nói, dễ mở rộng thành hội thoại qua lại.

1. Công thức nói về bất kỳ món ăn nào

Dùng 5 bước: What is it? → What is inside? → How do you eat it? → What does it taste like? → Is there something similar in your country?

This is called [dish].
It’s made with [ingredients].
You usually eat it with [side dish / sauce].
It tastes [crispy / fresh / rich / spicy / mild].
Do you have anything similar in France?

Từ vựng mô tả: crispy, crunchy, soft, tender, chewy, juicy, rich, light, fresh, mild, spicy, sweet, sour, salty, bitter, savory, smoky, creamy, refreshing, filling.

2. Bánh xèo

Từ vựng: Vietnamese savory pancake, fish sauce, dipping sauce, sweet-and-sour fish sauce, herbs, fresh herbs, lettuce, bean sprouts, shrimp/prawns, pork, beef, egg, mushrooms, vegetarian, crispy, wrap, dip.

Câu dễ nói:

  • This is bánh xèo.
  • It’s crispy on the outside.
  • You eat it with fresh herbs and lettuce.
  • You wrap a small piece with vegetables.
  • Then you dip it in the fish sauce.
  • There are many different kinds of herbs.
  • The vegetables make it feel lighter.
  • The herbs help balance the rich flavor.
  • This one has shrimp and pork.
  • You can also have beef, egg, seafood, or a vegetarian version.
  • The vegetarian one usually has mushrooms and vegetables.
  • After the meal, we often drink iced tea.

“Đỡ ngán”:

  • It feels lighter with the herbs.
  • The vegetables make it less heavy.
  • The herbs balance the richness.
  • It’s easier to eat with fresh vegetables.

Hội thoại:

You: Have you tried bánh xèo before?
Manager: No, first time.
You: It’s crispy, and you eat it with fresh herbs and lettuce.
Manager: How do I eat it?
You: Take a small piece, wrap it with vegetables, then dip it in the fish sauce.
Manager: There are a lot of herbs.
You: Yes. They make the dish feel lighter.
Manager: What’s inside?
You: This one has shrimp and pork, but there are many other versions too.

3. Phở

Từ vựng: beef broth, chicken broth, rice noodles, rare beef, brisket, beef balls, bean sprouts, lime, chili, herbs.

Câu:

  • The broth is the most important part.
  • It takes a long time to prepare.
  • You can add lime, chili, and herbs.
  • Some people like rare beef.
  • Others prefer well-cooked beef.
  • It’s light but still filling.
  • Many people eat pho for breakfast.

4. Bún chả / grilled pork noodles

Từ vựng: grilled pork, rice noodles, charcoal-grilled, smoky flavor, pickled vegetables, dipping sauce, fresh herbs.

  • The pork is grilled over charcoal.
  • It has a smoky flavor.
  • You eat it with noodles, herbs, and dipping sauce.
  • The pickled vegetables make it fresher.

Câu hỏi nối sang Pháp:

  • Do you have many grilled meat dishes in France?
  • Is barbecue common in summer?

5. Gỏi cuốn

Từ vựng: fresh spring rolls, rice paper, shrimp, pork, vermicelli, herbs, peanut sauce, fish sauce.

  • These are fresh spring rolls.
  • They’re not fried.
  • They’re quite light.
  • They’re wrapped in rice paper.
  • You can dip them in peanut sauce or fish sauce.

6. Cơm tấm

Từ vựng: broken rice, grilled pork chop, fried egg, shredded pork skin, pickled vegetables.

  • This is broken rice.
  • It usually comes with grilled pork and a fried egg.
  • It’s a very common lunch dish here.
  • It’s simple but very filling.

7. Bún bò Huế

Từ vựng: spicy beef noodle soup, lemongrass, chili, beef, pork, broth, herbs.

  • It’s a spicy beef noodle soup from Hue.
  • The broth has lemongrass and chili.
  • It’s stronger and spicier than pho.
  • If you like spicy food, you should try it.

8. Cao lầu / Mì Quảng

Cao lầu: thick noodles, pork, herbs, crispy crackers, local specialty.

Cao lau is a specialty from Hoi An. The noodles are thick and chewy. It comes with pork, herbs, and crispy crackers.

Mì Quảng: turmeric noodles, shrimp, pork, peanuts, herbs, small amount of broth.

Mi Quang is from central Vietnam. It has less broth than pho. It usually comes with shrimp, pork, herbs, and peanuts.

9. Lẩu

Từ vựng: hot pot, broth, seafood, beef, vegetables, mushrooms, cook at the table, share dishes.

  • Hot pot is good for sharing.
  • We cook everything at the table.
  • You can add seafood, beef, vegetables, and mushrooms.
  • It’s popular when we eat in a group.

Câu hỏi:

  • Do you often share dishes in France?
  • Or does everyone usually order their own plate?

10. Bánh mì – điểm giao thoa Việt–Pháp

Từ vựng: baguette, pork, pâté, pickled vegetables, cucumber, herbs, chili.

  • Banh mi uses a baguette, but the filling is very Vietnamese.
  • It usually has pork, pâté, pickled vegetables, cucumber, and herbs.
  • It’s a good example of Vietnamese and French food culture coming together.
  • The bread is French-inspired, but the flavors are very local.

Câu hỏi:

  • Does this remind you of sandwiches in France?
  • What kind of baguette sandwich is common in France?

11. Cà phê Việt Nam

Từ vựng: Vietnamese coffee, condensed milk, iced coffee, strong coffee, drip coffee, robusta.

  • Vietnamese coffee is quite strong.
  • This one has condensed milk.
  • We often drink it with ice.
  • The taste is stronger and sweeter than many European coffees.

Nối sang Pháp:

  • How do you usually drink coffee in France?
  • Espresso?
  • Do you drink coffee after lunch?
  • Is coffee after lunch common in France?

12. Trà đá

  • iced tea

  • unsweetened tea

  • refreshing

  • common with lunch

  • We often have iced tea with lunch.

  • It’s usually very light.

  • It’s refreshing in hot weather.

  • It’s very common in local restaurants.

13. Món chay Việt Nam

Từ vựng: vegetarian, vegan, tofu, mushrooms, vegetables, soy sauce, plant-based.

  • Vietnamese vegetarian food has a lot of variety.
  • Many dishes use tofu, mushrooms, and vegetables.
  • Some vegetarian dishes are made to look like meat dishes.
  • It can be very light and flavorful.

14. Hải sản Việt Nam

Từ vựng: squid, crab, shrimp, prawns, clams, oysters, scallops, grilled seafood, steamed seafood.

  • Seafood is very popular in coastal cities.
  • Grilled seafood is common in the evening.
  • Some places let you choose the seafood before they cook it.

15. Món đặc trưng của Pháp

Croissant: buttery, flaky, pastry, breakfast.

A croissant is light, buttery, and flaky. Do French people really eat croissants every morning?

Baguette: crusty, soft inside, bakery, fresh bread.

Is it common to buy fresh baguettes every day?

Cheese: soft cheese, hard cheese, blue cheese, goat cheese, strong smell, mild flavor, aged cheese.
Câu hỏi: What cheese would you recommend to a beginner? Which cheese has the strongest smell? Do you usually eat cheese before or after dessert?

Ratatouille: vegetables, zucchini, eggplant, tomato, herbs.
Coq au vin: chicken, red wine, slow-cooked.
Boeuf bourguignon: beef stew, red wine, slow-cooked, Burgundy.
Quiche: savory tart, eggs, cream, cheese, bacon.
Crêpe: thin pancake, sweet, savory, filling.

16. Điểm chung Việt–Pháp

  • Bánh mì ↔ baguette: ảnh hưởng Pháp trong ẩm thực Việt Nam.
  • Bánh xèo ↔ crêpe: cùng dạng pancake mỏng nhưng vị và texture khác.
  • Coffee culture: Việt Nam phổ biến cà phê đá; Pháp phổ biến espresso.
  • Pastry/cake culture: Việt Nam có nhiều bánh từ gạo; Pháp có nhiều pastry từ bơ và bột mì.

Câu:

  • Bánh xèo looks a little like a crêpe, but the taste is very different.
  • One is savory and crispy, while a French crêpe is usually softer.
  • We both have a strong food culture, but the ingredients are very different.

17. Câu hỏi mở về văn hóa ăn uống Pháp

  • What is your favorite French dish?
  • Which region has the best food?
  • What cheese would you recommend?
  • Do you drink wine with dinner often?
  • Is lunch still important in French work culture?
  • Do people take long lunch breaks?
  • What do you usually eat for Sunday lunch?
  • Do you cook at home often?
  • What dish do you miss most when you travel?
  • Do French people really eat bread every day?
  • What food is typical in your hometown?
  • Which dish should I try if I visit France?

18. Công thức nói về bất kỳ chuyến du lịch nào

Dùng 6 bước: Where is it? → Why is it special? → What can you do there? → When is the best time to go? → What should you eat there? → What should you be careful about?

[Place] is in [region].
It’s famous for [scenery / history / food].
You can [activity] there.
The best time to go is [season/month].
You should try [local dish].
Just be careful about [heat / rain / crowds / traffic].

19. Việt Nam theo vùng và mùa

Hà Nội

  • Old Quarter, Hoan Kiem Lake, Temple of Literature, street food, coffee culture.
  • Spring: pleasant, sometimes humid.
  • Summer: hot and humid.
  • Autumn: often very pleasant.
  • Winter: cool, sometimes cold.

Câu:

  • Autumn is a very nice time to visit Hanoi.
  • The weather is cooler and more comfortable.
  • The Old Quarter is good for walking and street food.

Hạ Long Bay

  • limestone islands, cruises, caves, sea views.
  • Ha Long Bay is famous for limestone islands.
  • Many people take an overnight cruise.

Ninh Bình

  • limestone mountains, rivers, boat trips, rice fields.
  • Ninh Binh is sometimes called “Ha Long Bay on land.”
  • A boat trip is one of the best ways to see the area.

Sapa

  • mountains, rice terraces, trekking, ethnic minority villages.
  • Cooler than lowland cities; can be foggy.
  • Sapa is much cooler than Ho Chi Minh City.
  • It’s good for trekking and mountain views.

Huế

  • Imperial City, royal cuisine, history.
  • Hue is a good place if you like history.
  • The food is also very different from southern Vietnamese food.

Đà Nẵng

  • beaches, seafood, Marble Mountains, easy access to Hoi An.
  • Da Nang is a good mix of city and beach.
  • It’s also close to Hoi An.

Hội An

  • ancient town, lanterns, food, riverside.
  • Hoi An is beautiful in the evening.
  • Cao lau is one of the local specialties.

Nha Trang

  • beach, seafood, islands.
  • Nha Trang is more focused on beaches and sea activities.

Đà Lạt

  • cool weather, coffee, flowers, hills, pine forests.
  • Da Lat is much cooler than Ho Chi Minh City.
  • It’s popular for coffee, flowers, and relaxing weekends.

Ho Chi Minh City

  • Ben Thanh Market, Nguyen Hue Walking Street, Central Post Office, Notre-Dame Cathedral area, food, nightlife.
  • Ho Chi Minh City is very lively.
  • Evening is better for walking because it’s cooler.

Mekong Delta

  • rivers, fruit, boats, local life.
  • The Mekong Delta is very different from the big cities.
  • You can see more rural life and river culture.

Phú Quốc

  • beaches, seafood, resorts, sunsets.
  • Phu Quoc is good for a relaxing beach holiday.
  • Seafood and sunsets are two of the main highlights.

20. Nói về thời tiết và mùa ở Việt Nam

  • The weather depends a lot on the region.
  • Northern Vietnam has four clearer seasons.
  • Southern Vietnam is more about dry season and rainy season.
  • Central Vietnam can get heavy rain later in the year.
  • You should check the weather before going to the coast.
  • In hot weather, early morning and evening are better for walking.

Công thức:

It’s usually [hot / cool / rainy / humid] at that time of year.
If you go in [month/season], you may get [rain / cooler weather / crowds].
I would recommend [morning/evening] for outdoor activities.

21. Công thức gợi ý địa điểm

If you like [beaches / food / history / mountains], you should visit [place].

Ví dụ:

  • If you like beaches, you should visit Da Nang or Phu Quoc.
  • If you like history, Hue is a good choice.
  • If you like mountains, Sapa is worth visiting.
  • If you like food and city life, Ho Chi Minh City is a good option.

22. Công thức hỏi về chuyến đi

  • Is this your first time here?
  • How long are you staying?
  • What have you seen so far?
  • Which place did you like most?
  • Did anything surprise you?
  • Was it too hot?
  • Was it crowded?
  • Did you try any local food?
  • Would you come back?
  • Where are you going next?

23. Chủ đề giao tiếp khác khi ăn trưa

Công việc nhẹ nhàng

  • What are you working on these days?
  • Which project is keeping you busiest?
  • Are you involved in many AI projects now?
  • Which use case do you find most useful?

Career

  • How did you get into this field?
  • Have you always worked in IT?
  • Which role did you enjoy most?
  • What was your first job?

Languages

  • How many languages do you speak?
  • Is English used a lot in your team?
  • I’ve started learning a little French.
  • Which French word should I learn first?

Work culture

  • Is lunch culture different in France?
  • Do people usually eat together at work?
  • Is remote work common in your team?
  • Do people start work early in France?

Weekend

  • Any plans for the weekend?
  • Do you usually stay in the city?
  • Do you prefer relaxing or going out?

Sports

  • Do you follow football?
  • Do you run or cycle?
  • Is rugby popular where you live?

Music / movies

  • What kind of music do you like?
  • Have you watched any good movies recently?
  • Do you prefer cinema or streaming?

24. Chủ đề khi đi uống tối

  • Long day.
  • That was a productive day.
  • We covered a lot today.
  • Now we can relax a bit.
  • Beer or wine?
  • Do you prefer red or white wine?
  • Would you like to try a local beer?
  • What do you usually drink in France?

Nói vui:

  • No more AI talk for one hour.
  • We can continue the technical discussion tomorrow.
  • This is the unofficial part of the workshop.

25. Tránh biến conversation thành phỏng vấn

Dùng công thức: Ask → React → Share → Follow up.

Ví dụ:

You: Do you like Vietnamese food?
Manager: Yes, especially pho.
You: Nice. Pho is one of my favorites too. I usually prefer beef pho. What about you?

26. Khi bí chủ đề

Các chủ đề an toàn: food, travel, weather, weekend, coffee, local culture, public transport, hobbies, sports, languages, work travel, AI trends, restaurants, cities, holidays, beaches, mountains, family activities, cooking, music.

27. 20 câu follow-up cực hữu ích

  • Really?
  • Why?
  • How was it?
  • Which one?
  • How often?
  • What happened next?
  • Did you enjoy it?
  • Would you do it again?
  • What about you?
  • What do you prefer?
  • Is that common in France?
  • Is it the same in Singapore?
  • What would you recommend?
  • When is the best time to go?
  • What should I try?
  • Was it difficult?
  • Was it expensive?
  • Was it crowded?
  • Did anything surprise you?
  • What did you like most?

28. 10 câu mô tả món ăn tự nhiên

  1. It’s crispy on the outside.
  2. It’s soft inside.
  3. It’s quite light.
  4. It’s a little rich.
  5. It’s not too spicy.
  6. The sauce is a bit sweet.
  7. The herbs make it fresher.
  8. It goes well with this sauce.
  9. It’s very filling.
  10. You should try this one.

29. 10 câu mô tả địa điểm

  1. It’s very lively.
  2. It’s quite peaceful.
  3. It can get crowded.
  4. It’s better in the evening.
  5. The view is beautiful.
  6. The food is great there.
  7. It’s easy to get around.
  8. It’s good for a short trip.
  9. It’s worth visiting.
  10. I would recommend it.

30. Mẫu hội thoại hoàn chỉnh

A. Bánh xèo

You: Have you tried bánh xèo before?
Manager: No. What is it?
You: It’s a crispy Vietnamese pancake.
Manager: What’s inside?
You: Usually shrimp, pork, and bean sprouts.
Manager: How do I eat it?
You: Wrap a small piece with herbs and lettuce, then dip it in the fish sauce.
Manager: Nice.
You: The herbs make it feel much lighter.

B. Phở

Manager: Is pho always beef?
You: No, there’s chicken pho too.
Manager: Which one do you prefer?
You: Beef. I like the broth more.
Manager: Is it spicy?
You: Not by default. You add chili yourself.

C. French cheese

You: What cheese would you recommend if I visit France?
Colleague: Maybe Comté to start.
You: Is it strong?
Colleague: Not too strong.
You: Good. I should probably not start with the strongest one.
Colleague: Definitely not.
You: Which one has the strongest smell?

D. Vietnam travel

Manager: If I have three free days, where should I go?
You: It depends on what you like.
Manager: Maybe beach and food.
You: Then Da Nang is a good choice. You can also visit Hoi An.
Manager: Is it far?
You: No, they’re quite close.

E. France travel

You: If I visit France for the first time, where should I go besides Paris?
Colleague: Maybe Lyon or Bordeaux.
You: Which one is better for food?
Colleague: Lyon.
You: Good to know. What should I eat there?

31. Cách luyện

Mỗi ngày chọn:

  • 1 món Việt
  • 1 món Pháp
  • 1 địa điểm
  • 5 câu hỏi follow-up

Luyện theo cách:

  1. Nói 30 giây về món ăn.
  2. Tự hỏi 3 câu.
  3. Tự trả lời.
  4. Nói lại không nhìn tài liệu.
  5. Hôm sau đổi chủ đề.

Mục tiêu: không dịch từng câu từ tiếng Việt trong đầu, mà học theo cụm.

MDTechnical_Advisor_Communication_Playbook_v2(1).mdCâu ngắn cho leaders, managers, AI transformation, TA · 1,120 lines⌄

Technical Advisor Communication Playbook

English for meetings, leaders, managers, lunch, dinner & social conversations

Mục tiêu: giao tiếp tự nhiên, ngắn gọn, dễ nói, ít bị vấp khi làm việc với leaders/managers ở Pháp, Singapore và đồng nghiệp quốc tế.

1. Nguyên tắc nói để không bị vấp

Ưu tiên câu ngắn. Thay vì nói một câu dài, chia ý:

I think AI can help a lot.
It can reduce manual work.
We can deliver more with the same team.
Then we can scale it to more projects.

Công thức an toàn: Point → Reason → Example → Question

Các câu đệm hữu ích:

  • Let me think.
  • From my side...
  • In our case...
  • For me, the key point is...
  • The main concern is...
  • One example is...
  • It depends.
  • I need to check.
  • I’ll confirm.
  • I’ll come back to you.

2. Small talk hằng ngày

Bắt đầu

  • Hi, how are you doing?
  • How’s your day going?
  • How have you been?
  • Did you have a good weekend?
  • Busy today?
  • How’s everything?
  • Good to see you again.
  • How was your morning?
  • Any plans for tonight?
  • How’s your week going?

Giữ câu chuyện tiếp tục

  • Really?
  • That sounds interesting.
  • That’s nice.
  • Good to know.
  • How was it?
  • What happened next?
  • Which one?
  • Why was that?
  • Did you enjoy it?
  • What about now?
  • What about you?

Kết thúc

  • It was nice talking with you.
  • See you later.
  • See you tomorrow.
  • Have a nice afternoon.
  • Have a good evening.
  • Take care.
  • Talk to you later.

3. Giao tiếp với leaders/managers

Báo cáo nhanh

  • Quick update from my side.
  • Everything is on track.
  • We have one blocker.
  • We are checking it now.
  • We expect to finish today.
  • We need one more day.
  • The issue is still there.
  • The deployment went well.
  • The test went well.
  • We got the expected result.

Khi chưa chắc

  • I need to check that.
  • I don’t have the full context yet.
  • Let me confirm with the team.
  • I’ll look into it.
  • I’ll come back with a clear answer.
  • We should check the risk before we decide.

Đưa recommendation

  • My suggestion is to start small.
  • I would test it first.
  • I think this is the safer option.
  • We should keep it simple.
  • We should avoid duplicate work.
  • We can reuse the same approach.
  • We should define a clear owner.
  • We need clear metrics.
  • We should measure the real value.

Challenge lịch sự

  • I have one concern.
  • Can we check one more point?
  • What is the main risk here?
  • Do we have another option?
  • What happens if this fails?
  • Can this scale?
  • Do we need this for all projects?
  • Is there a simpler way?
  • Can we reuse something we already have?

4. Technical Advisor English

  • From a technical point of view...
  • From my side...
  • The main risk is here.
  • We need to validate this first.
  • We should check the impact.
  • We need a clear owner.
  • We should keep this reusable.
  • We need common rules.
  • We should measure the outcome.
  • We need human review.
  • Security is important.
  • Data privacy is important.
  • We should keep the knowledge up to date.
  • We should make onboarding simple.
  • We need a feedback loop.

Khi bị so sánh với người cũ

  • He had a lot of experience in this area.
  • I’m still building the same level of context.
  • I’m getting up to speed on this topic.
  • I’m taking ownership of it.
  • I’m building a broader view across projects.
  • My focus is to identify technical risks early.
  • I’d like to understand where you expect me to bring the most value as TA.

5. AI Transformation / AI Adoption

Workflow hiện tại

  • We already have one common AI workflow for all projects.
  • It starts from the story.
  • Then we create the spec and plan.
  • After that, we move to implementation.
  • Then we use AI for code review and QC.
  • We also have BA and QC agents.
  • Each project has its own knowledge repository.

Common workflow + separate knowledge

  • The workflow is common across projects.
  • Each project keeps its own knowledge repository.
  • The project knowledge stays separate.
  • The common workflow uses project-specific context.
  • We should keep the project knowledge accurate and up to date.

Common workflow, separate knowledge.

Scale cross-project

  • The next step is to scale this to more projects.
  • We should make onboarding simple.
  • We should avoid too much manual setup.
  • If one project finds a better approach, the others should benefit too.
  • We should reuse what works.
  • We should avoid solving the same problem again and again.

Productivity

  • AI can help us deliver more with the same team.
  • We may need fewer extra resources.
  • AI can reduce manual work.
  • We should measure the real productivity gain.
  • We should compare before and after.
  • We should check time saved.
  • We should also check rework.
  • The goal is not only speed.
  • We need real value.

AI cost

  • The AI cost can also be high.
  • We should compare the productivity gain with the total cost.
  • We should look at the total cost, not only the AI cost.
  • If AI saves enough engineering time, the higher AI cost may still be worth it.
  • Can we compare delivery cost before and after AI adoption?
  • How do we measure the cost per story?
  • How do we measure the cost per feature?

More output with the same team is good, but we need to make sure the AI cost is justified.

Quality

  • We should not focus only on speed.
  • We also need to check quality.
  • We need clear quality gates.
  • AI should not stop at code generation.
  • We need review, test, and validation.
  • The final output still needs human approval.
  • We should compare defects before and after AI adoption.
  • We should also measure rework.

Governance & security

  • We need common rules.
  • We need approved tools.
  • We need security rules.
  • We need coding standards.
  • We need clear review steps.
  • What data can we share with AI?
  • What data should stay private?
  • We need human review for critical changes.

30-second contribution

We already have one common AI workflow for all projects.
Each project has its own knowledge repository.
Now we should measure the real value.
We should check time saved, quality, rework, and AI cost.
If the results are good, we can scale it to more projects.

60-second contribution

We already have one common AI workflow for all projects, which is a good starting point.
Each project keeps its own knowledge repository, so the workflow can stay common while the context stays project-specific.
For me, the next step is to measure the real value.
We should check time saved, quality, rework, and AI cost.
AI can help us deliver more with the same team, but we need to make sure the cost is still justified.
If one project finds a better way of using the workflow, that improvement should benefit the others.
Then we can scale with more confidence.

21. Mẫu đối thoại qua lại trong công việc

21.1. Daily/weekly update với manager

Manager: How are things going on your side?
You: Pretty good. We have one issue, but the team is already working on it.
Manager: Is it blocking the release?
You: Not for now. We still have some time.
Manager: Do you need any support?
You: Not yet. Let me check with the team first. If we need help, I’ll let you know.
Manager: Okay, keep me posted.
You: Sure, I will.

Biến thể

Manager: Any major risk this week?
You: The main risk is the deployment timeline.
Manager: Why?
You: We still need to validate one technical point.
Manager: When can you confirm?
You: I should have a clear answer by this afternoon.

21.2. Khi manager hỏi mà bạn chưa có câu trả lời

Manager: Do we know why this happened?
You: Not yet. I have a few ideas, but I need to confirm first.
Manager: What are you checking?
You: Mainly the logs and the recent changes.
Manager: When can you update us?
You: I’ll come back to you after I speak with the team.

Cách nói TA hơn

Manager: Do you think this is an infrastructure issue?
You: It could be, but I don’t want to jump to a conclusion.
Manager: What do you suggest?
You: Let’s check the application side and infrastructure side in parallel.
Manager: Sounds good.
You: I’ll coordinate with both teams.

21.3. Challenge một solution nhưng vẫn lịch sự

Architect: I think we should build a new service for this.
You: That could work. I have one concern, though.
Architect: What is it?
You: I’m not sure we need a new service for this use case.
Architect: Why not?
You: We may be able to reuse the existing component. It would be simpler to maintain.
Architect: Do you think it can scale?
You: I think so, but we should validate the load first.
Architect: Okay, let’s check that option.
You: Sure. I’ll prepare a quick comparison.

21.4. Khi bạn muốn đưa recommendation

Manager: What would you recommend?
You: I would start with the simpler option.
Manager: Why?
You: It has less impact and is easier to roll back.
Manager: What about performance?
You: We should test it, but I don’t expect a major issue.
Manager: Okay.
You: If the test is good, we can move forward with that option.

22. AI Transformation – đối thoại thực tế

22.1. Nói về workflow AI hiện tại

Manager: How do you see the current AI workflow?
You: I think the base is good. We already have one common flow for all projects.
Manager: What should we improve next?
You: For me, the next step is measurement.
Manager: Measurement of what?
You: Time saved, quality, rework, and AI cost.
Manager: Which one is the most important?
You: I would start with time saved and rework. They are easier to compare.
Manager: Makes sense.
You: Then we can add cost and quality metrics.

22.2. Nói về AI productivity

Leader: Do you think AI is really improving productivity?
You: Yes, but we need to measure it carefully.
Leader: What do you mean?
You: AI can help us deliver more with the same team, but it can also create rework if the output is not good.
Leader: So how should we measure it?
You: I would compare the time before and after AI adoption for the same type of task.
Leader: Anything else?
You: Yes, we should also track review findings and defects.

22.3. Nói về AI cost

Manager: The AI cost is getting high. Is it still worth it?
You: It depends on how much engineering time we save.
Manager: How can we prove that?
You: We can compare the delivery cost before and after AI adoption.
Manager: Per project?
You: I would start per story or per feature. It’s easier to compare.
Manager: Good idea.
You: Then we can see where AI gives the best return.

22.4. Scale từ 5 projects sang nhiều projects hơn

Leader: We have five projects using the workflow now. What should we do next?
You: I think we should learn from these five before scaling too fast.
Leader: What should we look at?
You: Which steps work well, where teams still need manual work, and where AI creates rework.
Leader: And after that?
You: We can simplify onboarding and roll it out to more projects.
Leader: Do we need a different workflow for each project?
You: No. The workflow can stay common. The project knowledge stays separate.

22.5. Knowledge repo riêng cho từng project

Manager: Why do we need a separate knowledge repository for each project?
You: Because each project has different business rules, architecture, and coding standards.
Manager: Does that make maintenance harder?
You: A little, but it keeps the context clean.
Manager: How do we avoid outdated knowledge?
You: We need clear ownership and regular updates.
Manager: Who should own it?
You: Ideally, the project team owns the content, and we define common guidance at TA level.

22.6. AI quality và human review

Leader: Can we trust AI output enough to reduce manual review?
You: For low-risk tasks, maybe.
Leader: What about production code?
You: I would still keep human review.
Leader: Even if the AI agent already did a code review?
You: Yes. AI can help us find issues, but the final decision should stay with the team.
Leader: So AI is more like an assistant?
You: Exactly. It helps us move faster, but it should not remove accountability.

23. Cross-project technical discussion

23.1. Khi một project muốn làm riêng

Project Lead: Our project is a bit different. We want our own solution.
You: I understand. What is the main difference?
Project Lead: We have a different architecture.
You: That makes sense. But maybe we can still reuse the common pattern.
Project Lead: Which part?
You: The workflow and governance can stay common. Only the project-specific implementation needs to change.
Project Lead: That could work.
You: Let’s identify what is really unique first.

23.2. Khi phát hiện duplicate work giữa projects

You: I noticed two teams are solving a very similar problem.
Manager: Which teams?
You: Project A and Project B.
Manager: Are they using the same approach?
You: Not exactly. That’s why I think we should compare them.
Manager: What do you suggest?
You: Let’s see if we can create one reusable pattern instead of maintaining two solutions.
Manager: Good point.
You: It could save time for future projects too.

You: Yes, I’ll send you the details after the meeting.

You: Mostly technical context, but some logs may contain sensitive information.
Security: Then we need clear rules.
You: Agreed. We should define what is allowed and what must be removed before sending anything to AI.
